claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that AI adoption will follow a standard technology S-curve: early adopters lead, laggards follow much later, and a segment of businesses never adopts at all — exactly as happened with the internet, which disrupted most industries yet left pockets of non-internet businesses that still operate profitably.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Some businesses will never adopt AI yet remain viable, so adoption is not universally required for survival

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that businesses which never adopt new technology (including AI) can still generate profit, citing as evidence businesses still using fax machines and paper clipboards for in-person-only operations that remain financially viable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Niche markets or local in-person businesses not competing on technology-enabled scale
bounded_by: Does not apply to businesses that compete directly against AI-augmented rivals at scale

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that throughout human history the competitive dynamic has been humans-with-better-tools beating humans-without-those-tools — and this same principle applies to AI: a service provider using AI to scale their output will outcompete one who does not.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Competition is human vs. human (not AI vs. human)
claims.mechanism: Superior tooling multiplies output per unit of human effort, creating an asymmetric competitive advantage for the tool user against peers operating without the tool.
bounded_by: Once competition shifts to AI vs. human (no human in the loop), this dynamic no longer protects the human

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that when the competitive frame shifts from human-with-AI versus human-without-AI to pure AI versus human, AI wins — making it existentially important for service providers to adopt AI while the human-vs-human frame still applies.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Competition has moved from human+tool vs. human to AI-only vs. human
claims.mechanism: AI systems operate faster, cheaper, and at greater scale than any individual human without augmentation, removing the human's inherent advantage in human-only competition.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for service providers (specifically citing a video editor as an example), AI does not threaten the job but instead provides leverage to multiply delivery scale — potentially 100x — making fear counterproductive and adoption urgent for short-to-medium term advantage.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Short to medium term (before AI vs. human competition frame becomes dominant)
Service providers competing against other humans
claims.mechanism: AI reduces manual overhead per deliverable, enabling the same human to produce far more output in the same time, expanding scale without proportional headcount cost.

numbers.axis: scale multiplier from AI adoption for service delivery

bounded_by: Applies to short-to-medium term only; long-run frame shifts to AI vs. human

examples.text: A video editor asked Alex Hormozi whether AI would eliminate their career. Hormozi reframed the threat: a video editor who uses AI to accelerate editing, asset generation, and iteration can serve far more clients than one who does not — making AI a scale lever rather than a job eliminator for the near term.

Hormozi cites fax-machine businesses and paper-clipboard-only in-person businesses as evidence that technology adoption is never universal. These operators never adopted the internet yet still generate profit, illustrating that laggards and non-adopters can survive in niches even as the broader market transforms.

practices.text: Harness AI as a leverage tool rather than fearing it — use it to multiply service delivery output while you still compete human-vs-human rather than waiting until AI-only competitors arrive.
